explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader, is the name the writer picks. Jesus was faithful to the One who appointed Him, just as Moses was faithful in all God's house. I bet the readers nodded right away, because nobody had to ask who he meant. Now the writer has a famous name to set Jesus beside.

Abraham, the man God told to leave his country (Genesis 12:1), is a giant in Israel's story, so I get why he came to mind. But the writer's name here is Moses. He says Jesus was faithful "just as Moses was faithful in all God’s house." Easy mix-up, friend. Plenty of big names were in that room.

David, Israel's king, is another famous name, and he'd get a crowd cheering. But he's not the one in this verse. The writer says Jesus was faithful "just as Moses was faithful in all God’s house." Moses is the name to hold onto for the rest of this passage.

explanations.answer: A builder honored above the house
explanations.explanation: That's the picture. The writer says the builder of a house has greater honor than the house itself, and that's how Jesus has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses. It's a simple image, and I like simple. A house is nice, but somebody had to build it.

explanations.answer: A shepherd honored above the sheep
explanations.explanation: I see why a shepherd came to mind. Jesus does call Himself the good shepherd (John 10:11). But that's not the picture in this passage. Here the writer talks about a builder and a house, and the builder gets the greater honor.

explanations.answer: A teacher honored above the student
explanations.explanation: A teacher is a nice picture, but the writer doesn't use it here. His picture is a house. The builder of a house has greater honor than the house itself, and that's how he explains Jesus' greater glory.
True. The writer says "every house is built by someone, but God is the builder of everything." That's a big sentence packed into one verse. Every house has a builder, and God is behind all of it.
This one is true, friend, so let's fix it. The writer says "every house is built by someone, but God is the builder of everything." Not just some things, everything. That's a lot of building.

explanations.answer: As the Son over God's house
explanations.explanation: Right on target. Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house, but "Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house." Servant in the house and Son over the house are two different spots. The writer wants us to see that difference.

Moses is the one the writer calls a servant, and he says so in verse 5. For Christ, the writer picks a different word. "Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house." So He's not standing beside Moses. He's the Son over the house.

explanations.answer: As a guest inside God's house
explanations.explanation: A guest is a fun guess, but the text has no guests here. Moses was faithful as a servant in all God's house. Christ "is faithful as the Son over God’s house." Son over the house, friend, and that's a big step up from visitor.
That's what the writer says: "And we are His house." He doesn't stop at telling us about Christ and Moses. He tells us where we fit in. It's good news, and I'm glad you caught it.
The temple is a natural guess, since it was a famous house for God. But the writer doesn't say it here. He says, "And we are His house." The house he's talking about is people, friend.
Heaven is a nice thought, but it isn't what this verse says. After saying Christ is faithful as the Son over God's house, the writer says, "And we are His house." So it's about us, not a place.

I can see why it reads that way, but it doesn't. The writer says "we are His house, if we hold firmly to our confidence and the hope of which we boast." There's an "if" in that sentence. So the answer is False, friend.

False is right. The writer says "we are His house, if we hold firmly to our confidence and the hope of which we boast." He doesn't say it happens whether we hold on or not. That little word "if" does a lot of work.
That's the warning. The Holy Spirit says, "Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts." Notice it starts with hearing His voice. Then comes the warning about what to do with it.
I get the guess, but that's not in these words. After "Today, if you hear His voice," the warning is "do not harden your hearts." The Holy Spirit is talking about the heart, not about leaders.
It does mention the past, so I see where that came from. But the warning itself is something else. The words say, "do not harden your hearts." The wilderness is what it points back to.
Forty years. The fathers tested and tried God "and for forty years saw My works." Forty years of seeing what God was doing. That's a long time to have front row seats.
Seven is a nice number, but it isn't the one in this verse. The text says the fathers tested and tried God, "and for forty years saw My works." Forty, friend. That's a lot more than seven.
Twelve shows up a lot in Scripture, so it's a fair guess. But this verse has a different number. The fathers "for forty years saw My works." That's forty years of seeing what God did.
That's the opposite of what God says. He says, "Their hearts are always going astray, and they have not known My ways." No starting to follow in that sentence. So the answer is False, friend.

False is right. God says of that generation, "Their hearts are always going astray, and they have not known My ways." Always going astray is the opposite of finally following. That's the reason He was angry with them.
His rest. God says, "They shall never enter My rest." It was a serious oath, sworn in anger. I think that's a heavy line, and it's worth slowing down for.
The temple is a natural guess, but it's not in this verse. God swears, "They shall never enter My rest." That's the word to remember. This part is heavy, friend.
A city is a reasonable guess, but the verse says something else. God swears, "They shall never enter My rest." He's the One who swore it. And I think it's a heavy line.

Unbelief. The writer warns about "a wicked heart of unbelief that turns away from the living God." He's talking to his own brothers now, not just to people long ago. The warning is for anyone, so he says, "See to it."

Pride is a real problem, and I've seen it in bakeries and everywhere else. But it's not the word in this verse. The writer warns about "a wicked heart of unbelief that turns away from the living God." Unbelief is the word he picks.

Fear is a fair guess, since plenty of hearts have it. But the writer uses a different word here. He warns about "a wicked heart of unbelief that turns away from the living God." Unbelief is what he's pointing at.

explanations.answer: Urge one another on every day
explanations.explanation: That's it. The writer says, "exhort one another daily, as long as it is called today." The reason he gives is "so that none of you may be hardened by sin’s deceitfulness." Notice the words "one another." It's a together job, friend.
Once a year is a lot slower than what the writer says. He says, "exhort one another daily, as long as it is called today." Daily, friend. Once a year would be a very long wait between encouragements.
Praying is a good thing, but that's not what the writer says here. He tells them to "exhort one another daily." The words are "one another," so he's pointing them toward each other.
True. The writer says to exhort one another daily "so that none of you may be hardened by sin’s deceitfulness." He says sin can be deceitful. That's why he tells them to look out for each other.

That one is true, friend. The writer says to exhort one another daily "so that none of you may be hardened by sin’s deceitfulness." That's his warning, and the daily encouragement is his answer to it.
To the end. The writer says, "We have come to share in Christ if we hold firmly to the end the assurance we had at first." Not just the start and not just the middle. Hold firmly all the way.
That would be nice, but it's not what the writer says. He says, "hold firmly to the end the assurance we had at first." To the end, friend. He doesn't mention things getting easier.
A single season is a lot shorter than what the writer says. He says to "hold firmly to the end the assurance we had at first." To the end is a whole lot longer than one season. It's the whole way.

explanations.answer: The people Moses led out of Egypt
explanations.explanation: Yes. The writer asks, "Were they not all those Moses led out of Egypt?" Moses was Israel's leader. The ones who heard and rebelled were the very people he led out.

explanations.answer: The people Joshua led into Canaan
explanations.explanation: Joshua, the man who took over leading after Moses (Deuteronomy 34:9), is a fair guess for a Bible name. But the writer doesn't name him here. He asks, "Were they not all those Moses led out of Egypt?" So the ones who heard and rebelled came out of Egypt with Moses.

explanations.answer: The people David led into Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: David, Israel's king, is a famous name, but the writer doesn't bring him up here. He asks, "Were they not all those Moses led out of Egypt?" So the ones who heard and rebelled are the people Moses led out.
That's his answer. The writer asks, "Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?" Forty years of anger, aimed at those who sinned. I think this part is heavy.

That's not in the text. The writer asks, "Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?" Those who sinned are the ones he names, so it's about the people in the wilderness. It's a heavy part, friend.
The text doesn't say that. The writer asks, "Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?" He names those who sinned. Anything beyond that, he leaves alone, and so will I.

True. The writer asks, "And to whom did He swear that they would never enter His rest? Was it not to those who disobeyed?" He asks a question where everybody already knows the answer. Those who disobeyed.
That one is true, friend. The writer asks, "And to whom did He swear that they would never enter His rest? Was it not to those who disobeyed?" The oath was sworn against those who disobeyed.
